title: Extending Kubernetes
subtitle: The API machinery, CRDs, controllers, operators and admission
description: Understand how Kubernetes is extended: the API machinery, custom resources, controllers and operators, admission control and the plugin interfaces for networking, storage and runtimes.
outcomes: Explain API groups, discovery, server-side apply, finalizers and ownerReferences
Design CRDs with validation schemas, printer columns and versions
Describe the reconcile loop and run controllers with leader election
Use operators such as cert-manager and CloudNativePG, and enforce policy with admission

modules.title: The API and custom resources
modules.summary: How the API server works and how to add new kinds to it.

lessons.title: The API machinery
lessons.summary: Groups, versions and resources, discovery, server-side apply, field managers, ownerReferences and finalizers.
objectives: Read an apiVersion as group/version and find resources with kubectl api-resources
Explain server-side apply and field ownership
Use ownerReferences and finalizers to understand garbage collection and stuck deletions

sections.title: Everything is a resource in an API group
sections.body:
The Kubernetes API server is a REST API. Every object lives at a path built from its **group**, **version** and **resource** (the plural lowercase name). The core group (empty name) is served under `/api/v1`, every other group under `/apis/<group>/<version>`. In a manifest, `apiVersion: apps/v1` means group `apps`, version `v1`; `apiVersion: v1` means the core group.

Versions signal stability: `v1alpha1` is experimental and usually off by default, `v1beta1` is pre-release, `v1` is stable. etcd stores each object in exactly one **storage version**, and the API server converts to whichever version a client asks for. Custom resources, added later in this course, join this same machinery and get the same paths, RBAC, watches and `kubectl` support.

sections.title: Request paths and the metadata fields that drive lifecycle
head: Item
Value or setter
Purpose
Example
rows: group apps, version v1, resource deployments
core group has no name and lives under /api
custom resources look exactly like built-in ones
tracks which field manager owns each field (server-side apply)
declares the parent; deleting it garbage-collects the child
blocks removal until cleanup is done
set when a delete is requested but finalizers remain
increments on spec change, compared with status.observedGeneration

sections.title: About this example: discovering what the API serves
sections.body: These read-only commands ask the API server what it offers, so they are safe on any cluster. `kubectl api-resources` lists each resource with its short name, group, kind and whether it is namespaced; `kubectl api-versions` lists group/version pairs; `kubectl get --raw` sends a raw authenticated GET and shows the discovery document kubectl itself caches. Look at `APIVERSION` and `NAMESPACED` in the table and at the `verbs` array in the JSON.

sections.title: Discovery commands
sections.code:
kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps
kubectl api-versions | head -6
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy
kubectl get --raw /apis/apps/v1 | head -c 300
sections.output:

sections.title: About this example: server-side apply and a field conflict
sections.body: Classic client-side apply stores the last manifest in an annotation and computes a three-way patch in kubectl. **Server-side apply** moves that logic into the API server, which records an owner (the **field manager**) for every field in `managedFields`. In this session we apply a ConfigMap as `team-a`, then try to change `LOG_LEVEL` as `team-b`; the server refuses with a conflict instead of overwriting. Read the error text, which names the field and the current owner, and the `managedFields` entry afterwards.

sections.title: Applying with named field managers
sections.code:
cat > cm.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: ssa-demo
  namespace: default
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  REGION: eu-west-1
EOF
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=team-a -f cm.yaml
sed -i 's/info/debug/' cm.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=team-b -f cm.yaml
kubectl get cm ssa-demo --show-managed-fields -o yaml | sed -n '1,18p'
sections.output:
configmap/ssa-demo serverside-applied
Apply failed with 1 conflict: conflict with "team-a": .data.LOG_LEVEL
Please review the fields above--they currently have other managers. Here
are the ways you can resolve this warning:
* If you intend to manage all of these fields, please re-run the apply
  command with the `--force-conflicts` flag.
* If you do not intend to manage all of the fields, please edit your
  manifest to remove references to the fields that should keep their
  current managers.

apiVersion: v1
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  REGION: eu-west-1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  managedFields:
  - apiVersion: v1
    fieldsType: FieldsV1
    fieldsV1:
      f:data:
        f:LOG_LEVEL: {}
        f:REGION: {}
    manager: team-a
    operation: Apply
    time: "2026-11-13T09:12:44Z"
sections.note: Controllers should use server-side apply with one stable --field-manager name, so humans and automation can share an object without clobbering each other.

sections.title: About this example: an object guarded by a finalizer
sections.body: This ConfigMap carries a **finalizer** named `example.com/cleanup`. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f`, then run `kubectl delete cm protected`: the API server only sets `deletionTimestamp`, and the object stays in Terminating state until whatever controller owns that finalizer finishes cleanup and removes it. Here no controller exists, so you play the controller in the exercise. Compare this with `ownerReferences`, which is how a ReplicaSet's Pods are removed when the ReplicaSet goes away.

sections.title: Object with a finalizer
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: protected
  namespace: default
  finalizers:
  - example.com/cleanup
data:
  note: "deletion waits until example.com/cleanup is removed"
sections.note: After a delete, kubectl get cm protected -o jsonpath='{.metadata.deletionTimestamp}' prints a timestamp while the object is still present.

sections.title: Do not strip finalizers casually
sections.body: A namespace stuck in Terminating usually has a finalizer from an unavailable controller or an API service that is down. Find the real cause first (`kubectl get apiservice`, controller logs). Removing a finalizer with `kubectl patch ... -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' --type=merge` skips the cleanup it protected and can leak load balancers, disks or DNS records.

exercises.title: Find where a resource lives
exercises.prompt: Find the group, version and namespaced flag for CronJobs.
exercises.expected: A row with cronjobs, short name cj, APIVERSION batch/v1, NAMESPACED true.

exercises.title: Release a stuck deletion
exercises.prompt: Apply the finalizer ConfigMap, delete it, confirm it lingers, then act as the controller and remove the finalizer.
exercises.command: kubectl delete cm protected --wait=false && kubectl get cm protected -o jsonpath='{.metadata.deletionTimestamp}'
exercises.expected: A deletionTimestamp is printed and the object remains until the finalizer is patched away.
exercises.hint: A merge patch with finalizers set to null clears the list.

questions.question: What does apiVersion: apps/v1 mean?
questions.explain: The part before the slash is the API group, the part after is the version. The core group has no prefix.

questions.question: What does a field conflict in server-side apply tell you?
options: Another manager owns a field you tried to set to a different value
questions.explain: SSA tracks ownership in managedFields and refuses to silently overwrite another manager's value.

questions.question: An object was deleted but remains with a deletionTimestamp. Why?
questions.explain: Finalizers keep the object present until the owning controller completes cleanup and removes them.

questions.question: What happens to children when their owner (via ownerReferences) is deleted by default?
options: They move to the default namespace
questions.explain: The garbage collector deletes dependents whose owner no longer exists.

lessons.title: CustomResourceDefinitions
lessons.summary: Teach the API server a new kind: CRD anatomy, OpenAPI validation, defaults, printer columns, status subresource and versions.
objectives: Write a complete CRD with a structural schema
Validate and default custom resources with OpenAPI v3 and enums
Show custom columns and plan multi-version CRDs

sections.title: A CRD adds a new REST resource to the API server
sections.body:
A **CustomResourceDefinition** (CRD) is itself an object in the `apiextensions.k8s.io/v1` group. When you create one, the API server immediately starts serving a new endpoint such as `/apis/data.example.com/v1/namespaces/*/backups`, stores the objects in etcd, and makes them work with `kubectl`, RBAC, watches, labels and `kubectl explain`. No server code is compiled in; the CRD only describes the shape.

A CRD on its own does **nothing** beyond storing data. Behavior comes from a controller that watches those objects, covered in the next lessons. Think of a CRD as the schema of a table and the controller as the application using it.

sections.title: Key CRD fields
head: Field
Meaning
Example
rows: API group, usually a DNS domain you own
CamelCase kind and lowercase plural used in the URL
Served to clients; exactly one version is the storage version
Structural schema used for validation, defaulting and pruning
Separate /status endpoint so controllers and users do not collide
Extra columns for kubectl get, each with a jsonPath

sections.title: About this example: the Backup CRD
sections.body: This is a complete CRD defining a `Backup` kind in group `data.example.com`, intended to describe a scheduled database backup. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f backup-crd.yaml`. Look at the `schema` block, where `required`, `minLength`, `pattern`, `minimum`/`maximum`, `enum` and `default` do the validation, and at `additionalPrinterColumns`, which controls what `kubectl get backups` prints.

sections.title: backup-crd.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: backups.data.example.com
spec:
  group: data.example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: backups
    singular: backup
    kind: Backup
    shortNames:
    - bkp
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    subresources:
      status: {}
    additionalPrinterColumns:
    - name: Database
      type: string
      jsonPath: .spec.database
    - name: Schedule
      type: string
      jsonPath: .spec.schedule
    - name: Phase
      type: string
      jsonPath: .status.phase
    - name: Age
      type: date
      jsonPath: .metadata.creationTimestamp
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        required: ["spec"]
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            required: ["database", "schedule"]
            properties:
              database:
                type: string
                minLength: 1
              schedule:
                type: string
                pattern: '^(\S+\s+){4}\S+$'
              retention:
                type: integer
                minimum: 1
                maximum: 90
                default: 7
              storageClass:
                type: string
                enum: ["standard", "fast", "archive"]
          status:
            type: object
            properties:
              phase:
                type: string
              lastSuccess:
                type: string
                format: date-time
sections.note: Schemas must be structural: every field needs a type. Unknown fields are pruned unless x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields is set.

sections.title: About this example: a Backup custom resource
sections.body: This is an instance of the new kind, created with `kubectl apply -f orders-backup.yaml` after the CRD is established. It sets only `database`, `schedule` and `storageClass`; the API server fills `retention: 7` from the schema default. Look at `apiVersion: data.example.com/v1` and `kind: Backup`, which must match the CRD's group, version and names.

sections.title: orders-backup.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: data.example.com/v1
kind: Backup
metadata:
  name: orders-nightly
  namespace: default
spec:
  database: orders
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  storageClass: fast

sections.title: About this example: applying, listing and being rejected
sections.body: This session installs the CRD, creates the resource, lists it using the short name and printer columns, and then tries an invalid object to prove validation works. `kubectl get crd` shows the established CRD. In the final error, read the field path (`spec.storageClass`) and the supported values, which come straight from the schema enum.

sections.title: Install and validate
sections.code:
kubectl apply -f backup-crd.yaml
kubectl apply -f orders-backup.yaml
kubectl get bkp
kubectl get backup orders-nightly -o jsonpath='{.spec.retention}{"\n"}'
kubectl patch backup orders-nightly --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"storageClass":"tape"}}'
sections.output:
customresourcedefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io/backups.data.example.com created
backup.data.example.com/orders-nightly created
NAME             DATABASE   SCHEDULE    PHASE   AGE
orders-nightly   orders     0 2 * * *           5s
7
The Backup "orders-nightly" is invalid: spec.storageClass: Unsupported value: "tape": supported values: "standard", "fast", "archive"

sections.title: Versions, conversion and removal
sections.body:
A CRD can serve several versions at once, for example `v1beta1` and `v1`. Only one is the **storage** version; clients can read any served version. If the schemas differ, set `spec.conversion` to `Webhook` and run a conversion service; if they are identical the default `None` strategy just rewrites `apiVersion`.

The safe lifecycle is: add `v1`, make it the storage version, run `kubectl get backups -A -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -` style migration (or the Storage Version Migrator), then set `served: false` on the old version, and finally remove it from `status.storedVersions`. Deleting a CRD **deletes every custom resource of that kind**, so protect CRDs in production with RBAC and backups.

For rules beyond OpenAPI keywords, use `x-kubernetes-validations` with CEL, for example `rule: "self.retention <= 30 || self.storageClass == 'archive'"`; it runs inside the API server with no webhook.

exercises.title: Inspect your CRD with explain
exercises.prompt: Use kubectl explain on the new kind to read the schema you defined.
exercises.expected: Fields database, schedule, retention and storageClass are listed with their types.
exercises.hint: explain works for custom kinds once the CRD is established.

exercises.title: Break validation on purpose
exercises.prompt: Try to create a Backup with retention 500.
exercises.expected: An error that spec.retention must be less than or equal to 90.

questions.question: What does creating a CRD alone give you?
options: A new API endpoint storing objects, with no behavior
questions.explain: A CRD only adds the resource type. A controller must act on the objects.

questions.question: Which CRD field controls extra columns in kubectl get?
questions.explain: additionalPrinterColumns maps a jsonPath to a column.

questions.question: What happens to custom resources when their CRD is deleted?
questions.explain: Removing the CRD removes the endpoint and all stored objects of that kind.

questions.question: How many versions of a CRD can be the storage version?
questions.explain: Exactly one version has storage: true, though several can be served.

modules.title: Controllers, operators and admission
modules.summary: Automate with reconcile loops, use operators and guard the API.

lessons.title: Controllers and the reconcile loop
lessons.summary: How controllers converge actual state to desired state: informers, caches, work queues, idempotent reconcile and leader election.
objectives: Describe the observe-diff-act loop and why it is level-triggered
Name the roles of informer, cache, work queue and reconciler
Run controllers with leader election and read Lease objects

sections.title: Level-triggered control: converge, never replay events
sections.body:
A **controller** is a loop that watches objects and works to make the real world match the `spec`. The Deployment controller, the Job controller and every operator are built this way. The key property is that controllers are **level-triggered**: the reconciler is handed the *name* of an object, re-reads the current state and decides what to do, rather than replaying a list of past events. If an event is missed or a pod restarts, the next reconcile still converges.

This forces two rules. Reconcile must be **idempotent** (running it ten times equals running it once), and it must not depend on which event woke it up. Failures are returned as errors, and the work queue retries them with exponential backoff.

sections.title: Moving parts of a controller built with client-go or controller-runtime
head: Component
Job
Example
rows: Does one LIST then a WATCH against the API server and feeds a local cache
Local read-only copy so reconcile reads do not hit the API server
Turn add/update/delete into queue keys, often filtered by predicates
Deduplicates keys, rate-limits, retries with backoff
Ten changes to one Backup become one item
Your function: read, diff, create/update/delete, update status
Link children to the parent so deletion cascades and child events map to the parent
Only one replica runs the loop at a time

sections.title: About this example: a reconciler in Go
sections.body: This is a fragment of a controller-runtime reconciler for the Backup CRD from the previous lesson, shown as plain text because it is Go source and not a manifest. It reads the Backup, checks whether the owned CronJob exists, creates it if not, writes `.status.phase`, and requeues after ten minutes. Look at the three numbered comments (observe, diff and act, report) and at `SetControllerReference`, which makes the CronJob garbage-collected with its Backup.

sections.title: BackupReconciler.Reconcile (Go, abridged)
sections.note: Return an error to retry with backoff, ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: d} to look again later, and an empty Result when converged.

sections.title: About this example: running a controller with two replicas
sections.body: This Deployment runs the controller with two replicas for availability. Both pods watch the API, but `--leader-elect=true` makes them compete for a Lease so only one reconciles at a time; the other is a hot standby. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f backup-controller.yaml`. Look at `--leader-election-id`, the health endpoints used by the probes, and the memory limit sized for an informer cache. The image name is an example; substitute your own controller image.

sections.title: backup-controller.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backup-controller
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: backup-controller
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backup-controller
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backup-controller
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: default
      containers:
      - name: manager
        image: registry.example.com/backup-controller:1.4.2
        args:
        - --leader-elect=true
        - --leader-election-id=backup-controller.data.example.com
        - --metrics-bind-address=:8080
        - --health-probe-bind-address=:8081
        ports:
        - name: metrics
          containerPort: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8081
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 8081
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 50m
            memory: 64Mi
          limits:
            memory: 128Mi
sections.note: In a real install the ServiceAccount also needs RBAC to list/watch backups and manage cronjobs, plus coordination.k8s.io leases.

sections.title: About this example: observing leader election and reconciles
sections.body: The Lease is a small object in the `coordination.k8s.io` group that the leader renews every few seconds; `holderIdentity` names the winner. This session shows the Lease, the controller logs with the election and a reconcile, and what happens after the leader pod is deleted. Look at `holderIdentity` changing and at `renewTime`, which should stay within a few seconds of now.

sections.title: Common controller bugs
sections.body: Watch for: acting on stale cache reads right after a write (re-fetch or tolerate conflicts), forgetting `status.observedGeneration`, non-idempotent creates that fail with AlreadyExists, hot loops caused by writing status on every reconcile, and updating `spec` when you meant to update only `status`. Use finalizers for external cleanup, and ownerReferences for in-cluster children. Most teams generate the scaffolding with kubebuilder or Operator SDK (controller-runtime); kopf and the Java Operator SDK exist for Python and Java.

exercises.title: Watch a controller work
exercises.prompt: Scale a Deployment and observe the ReplicaSet controller converge it.
exercises.command: kubectl scale deployment backup-controller --replicas=3 && kubectl get pods -l app=backup-controller -w
exercises.expected: New pods appear until the count equals 3 without any further input.
exercises.hint: The Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers do the reconciling.

exercises.title: Find the current leader
exercises.prompt: Read the holderIdentity of a controller Lease.
exercises.command: kubectl get lease -n kube-system kube-controller-manager -o jsonpath='{.spec.holderIdentity}'
exercises.expected: The name of the control-plane node and unique id currently leading.
exercises.hint: Leases are in coordination.k8s.io; the built-in ones live in kube-system.

questions.question: Why must a reconcile function be idempotent?
options: It may run many times for the same object and must converge safely
questions.explain: Level-triggered controllers can reconcile repeatedly due to resyncs, retries and duplicate events.

questions.question: What does the work queue provide?
options: Deduplication, rate limiting and retry with backoff
questions.explain: Many events for one key collapse into one item, and failed items are retried with backoff.

questions.question: What does leader election with a Lease achieve for a 2-replica controller?
options: Only one active reconciler, with a standby ready
questions.explain: Only the Lease holder runs the loop, which avoids conflicting writes.

questions.question: Why does a controller read from an informer cache instead of the API server?
options: It reduces API server load and latency
questions.explain: The cache is populated by LIST+WATCH and serves reads locally, though it can briefly lag behind writes.

lessons.title: The operator pattern and real operators
lessons.summary: CRD plus controller equals an operator: install and use cert-manager and CloudNativePG, and judge operators before adopting them.
objectives: Define an operator as domain knowledge encoded in a CRD and controller
Install operators with Helm and drive them with custom resources
Evaluate an operator for maturity, upgrades and failure modes

sections.title: Operators encode what a human operator would do
sections.body:
An **operator** is a CRD plus a controller that automates the lifecycle of a piece of software: install, configure, scale, back up, upgrade and recover. Instead of a runbook saying 'promote a replica, repoint the service, reattach storage', you declare `instances: 3` on a database object and the operator performs the steps, reconciling continuously.

In practice you consume operators far more often than you write them. You install the operator once (CRDs, a Deployment, RBAC), then create small custom resources, and `kubectl get`, `describe` and events work as for built-in kinds.

sections.title: Operators you will meet
head: Operator
CRDs (examples)
What it automates
Typical install
rows: Issues and renews TLS certificates (ACME, Vault, internal CA) into Secrets
PostgreSQL HA, failover, backups, rolling upgrades
helm or kubectl apply of release manifest
Runs Prometheus and generates scrape config from CRs
GitOps sync of manifests to clusters

sections.title: About this example: cert-manager issuer and certificate
sections.body: One file with two custom resources. The `ClusterIssuer` tells cert-manager how to obtain certificates (here the Let's Encrypt staging ACME server using HTTP-01 through the nginx ingress class). The `Certificate` asks for a certificate for two DNS names, renewing 15 days before expiry, and stores it in Secret `shop-tls`. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f shop-tls.yaml` after cert-manager is installed; look at `issuerRef` and `secretName`, which your Ingress then consumes.

sections.title: shop-tls.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-staging
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-staging-account-key
    solvers:
    - http01:
        ingress:
          ingressClassName: nginx
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: shop-tls
  namespace: default
spec:
  secretName: shop-tls
  duration: 2160h
  renewBefore: 360h
  dnsNames:
  - shop.example.com
  - www.shop.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-staging
    kind: ClusterIssuer
sections.note: Switch to the production ACME URL only after staging works; production has strict rate limits.

sections.title: About this example: a PostgreSQL cluster with CloudNativePG
sections.body: This single `Cluster` object makes the operator create three PostgreSQL pods (one primary, two streaming replicas), their PVCs, services (`-rw`, `-ro`, `-r`) and credentials Secret. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f orders-db.yaml` once the operator is running. Look at `instances`, which you change to scale, `storage.size`, and `bootstrap.initdb`, which creates the first database and owner.

sections.title: orders-db.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1

sections.title: About this example: installing operators and reading their status
sections.body: This session installs both operators from their Helm charts, then inspects the results. Operators put progress in `status` and `Ready` conditions, so `kubectl get` is your first check. In the output, compare the `READY` and `STATUS` columns of the certificate and the cluster, and note `kubectl cnpg status` is a plugin that gives richer detail.

sections.title: Install and inspect
sections.code:
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io && helm repo add cnpg https://cloudnative-pg.github.io/charts
helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set crds.enabled=true
helm install cnpg cnpg/cloudnative-pg -n cnpg-system --create-namespace
kubectl apply -f shop-tls.yaml -f orders-db.yaml
kubectl get certificate,cluster
kubectl get pods -l cnpg.io/cluster=orders-db

sections.title: Operator adoption checklist
sections.body: Before adopting: check the project's maturity and release cadence, how CRD upgrades are handled (Helm does not upgrade CRDs in `crds/` after install), what happens if the operator is down (managed workloads usually keep running), backup and restore for stateful operators, resource requests of the operator itself, and RBAC it requests. Pin versions and test upgrades in staging, and never delete a CRD to 'reset' an operator, since that deletes all its data objects.

exercises.hint: CRDs are cluster-scoped objects whose names end with their group.

questions.question: What defines an operator?
options: A CRD plus a controller encoding operational knowledge
questions.explain: The operator pattern pairs custom resources with a controller that automates lifecycle tasks.

questions.question: In the cert-manager example, where does the issued certificate end up?
options: In the Secret named by spec.secretName
questions.explain: cert-manager writes tls.crt and tls.key into the Secret you name.

questions.question: If the operator Deployment is down, what usually happens to workloads it created?
options: They keep running but are no longer reconciled
questions.explain: Pods and Services exist independently; only automation (failover, renewal) stops until the operator returns.

questions.question: Why be careful with CRD upgrades from Helm?
options: Helm does not upgrade CRDs in the crds/ directory, so they can lag behind the operator
questions.explain: Helm installs crds/ once and skips them on upgrade, so many charts document a separate CRD upgrade step.

lessons.title: Admission, aggregation and extension points
lessons.summary: Intercept requests with admission policies and webhooks, extend the API with aggregation, and map the CNI, CSI, CRI and device plugin interfaces.
objectives: Place mutating and validating admission in the request flow
Write a native ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and a webhook configuration safely
Choose between CRDs, API aggregation and node-level plugin interfaces

sections.title: Admission control sits between authorization and etcd
sections.body:
Every write to the API server passes through authentication, authorization (RBAC), then **admission**, then schema validation and persistence. Admission has two phases: **mutating** admission can change the object (inject a sidecar, set defaults), then **validating** admission can only accept or reject it. Built-in admission plugins such as LimitRanger and ResourceQuota run here, and you can add your own in two ways.

The modern option is **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy** (GA in v1.30): CEL expressions run inside the API server with no extra service. The classic option is a **webhook**: the API server POSTs an `AdmissionReview` to your HTTPS service, which answers allowed or denied (and for mutation, a JSON patch). Webhooks are powerful but become part of your cluster's availability path.

sections.title: About this example: a native admission policy
sections.body: This pair of objects blocks creation of Deployments without a `team` label, but only in namespaces labeled `env=prod`. The `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` holds the rule as a CEL `expression`; the binding selects where it applies and sets `validationActions: [Deny]` (use `Warn` or `Audit` first to roll out safely). Apply the file with `kubectl apply -f policy.yaml` and look at `matchConstraints`, `expression` and `message`.

sections.title: policy.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups: ["apps"]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
  - expression: "has(object.metadata.labels) && 'team' in object.metadata.labels"
    message: "Deployments must carry a 'team' label"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: require-team-label-prod
spec:
  policyName: require-team-label
  validationActions: ["Deny"]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        env: prod
sections.note: Start with validationActions: [Warn, Audit] to see violations in client warnings and audit logs before enforcing.

sections.title: About this example: a validating webhook registration
sections.body: This registers an external webhook that is called for every Pod CREATE except in `kube-system` and `policy-system`, and the exclusion of its own namespace is essential. `failurePolicy: Fail` rejects pods when the webhook is unreachable, which is safer for security but can block the whole cluster; `timeoutSeconds: 5` bounds the damage. The CA bundle is injected by cert-manager through the annotation. Look at `rules`, `namespaceSelector` and `clientConfig.service`.

sections.title: image-policy-webhook.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: image-policy.example.com
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/inject-ca-from: policy-system/image-policy-cert
webhooks:
- name: images.policy.example.com
  admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
  sideEffects: None
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failurePolicy: Fail
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations: ["CREATE"]
    resources: ["pods"]
  namespaceSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
      operator: NotIn
      values: ["kube-system", "policy-system"]
  clientConfig:
    service:
      namespace: policy-system
      name: image-policy
      path: /validate
      port: 443
sections.note: The backing Deployment and Service (image-policy in policy-system) must exist and serve HTTPS /validate before this is applied.

sections.title: About this example: seeing denials and aggregated APIs
sections.body: This session creates a Deployment without the label in a prod namespace to see the policy message, then lists APIService objects, which is how aggregated APIs are registered. In the `APIService` list, `Local` means the built-in server answers, while an entry with a service name (such as metrics-server) is aggregated; its `AVAILABLE` column must be `True` or discovery and namespace deletion can hang.

sections.title: Webhooks can take down a cluster
sections.body: A Fail-closed webhook whose pods are themselves blocked by that webhook creates a deadlock. Always exclude the webhook's namespace and `kube-system`, run at least two replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget, keep `timeoutSeconds` low, avoid matching `*` resources, and prefer ValidatingAdmissionPolicy when CEL is enough. Recovery from a broken webhook is `kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>`.

questions.question: What is the order of API request handling?
questions.explain: The request is authenticated, authorized, then passes mutating and validating admission before being stored.

questions.question: Which phase can modify an object?
questions.explain: Mutating webhooks run first and can patch the object; validating ones only allow or deny.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of ValidatingAdmissionPolicy over a webhook?
options: It runs CEL in the API server with no extra service to operate
questions.explain: There is no network hop or service to keep available.

questions.question: Which extension point lets you advertise GPUs to the scheduler?
questions.explain: Device plugins register extended resources like nvidia.com/gpu with the kubelet.
